title: Keyword Density Checker: how it works, formula and examples

content:
The [Keyword Density Checker](/keyword-density-checker) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Keyword density and word count from a URL or pasted text. Enter your keyword or phrase and text to analyse (or a URL — choose below) and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Measure keyword density: how often a word or phrase appears in a piece of text, as a percentage of all words. Enter a keyword and either paste text or fetch a live page by URL, and the tool reports the word count, the number of times the keyword appears, its density, and the most common words in the text. Density of 1–2% is the usual rough guide for a target keyword — far above that usually reads as stuffing. Pasted text never leaves your browser; only URL mode fetches from the server.

## How to use the Keyword Density Checker

Start by typing or pasting your keyword or phrase, then typing or pasting your text to analyse (or a URL — choose below). The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause.

1. Enter the keyword or phrase you want to measure.
2. Paste the text, or switch to URL mode and enter a page address.
3. Read the density, the word count and the most common words.

## Formula

Density = (times the keyword appears ÷ total words) × 100. For example, a keyword appearing 6 times in 300 words has a density of 2%.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Keyword Density Checker](/keyword-density-checker) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. A 300-word text mentioning “calculator” 6 times has a keyword density of 2% — inside the usual 1–2% guide range. Try the same figures in the [Keyword Density Checker](/keyword-density-checker) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## Trying it out

The fastest way to see what the [Keyword Density Checker](/keyword-density-checker) does is to open it and enter values you already know the answer for. Change one input at a time and watch how the result responds — that tells you more than any description. Everything runs in your browser, so you can experiment freely: nothing is saved, sent or tracked.

## What density is “right”?

There is no official number — Google has never published one. The old rule of thumb is 1–2% for a target keyword: enough that the page is clearly about the topic, not so much that it reads unnaturally. Above 3–4% usually means the keyword is being repeated for the search engine rather than the reader, which is what keyword stuffing looks like. The most useful check is often the top-words list: if the top words are not your topic, the page is probably not about what you think it is.

## Pasted text vs. a live URL

Pasted text is analysed in your browser and never leaves your device — use it for drafts. URL mode fetches the live page from the server and analyses the visible text (scripts and styles are ignored). The two can differ: a live page includes navigation, footers and sidebars, which dilute the density of the article itself.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- Aim for roughly 1–2% for a target keyword — more usually reads as stuffing.
- Check the top-words list: it should be your topic, not your navigation.
- Use pasted text for drafts — it never leaves your browser.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is keyword density?

How often a word or phrase appears in a text, as a percentage of all words. A keyword appearing 6 times in 300 words has a density of 2%. Try it with your own numbers in the [Keyword Density Checker](/keyword-density-checker) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What is a good keyword density?

There is no official number, but 1–2% is the usual rough guide. Much above 3–4% usually reads as keyword stuffing. Try it with your own numbers in the [Keyword Density Checker](/keyword-density-checker) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Does keyword density still matter for SEO?

Less than it used to — search engines now understand topics, not just exact words. It is still a useful check that a page is actually about its target keyword. Try it with your own numbers in the [Keyword Density Checker](/keyword-density-checker) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Is my pasted text uploaded anywhere?

No. Pasted text is analysed in your browser and never leaves your device. Only URL mode fetches anything, from the server. Try it with your own numbers in the [Keyword Density Checker](/keyword-density-checker) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.
